name: C-Tactile Affective Touch Pathway in Architectural Material Experience
short_description: Architectural surfaces engage dual somatosensory pathways; CT afferents evaluate body-surface contact for optimal temperature, velocity, and roughness
structural_pattern: Architectural surfaces that make contact with the body engage two parallel somatosensory pathways. The discriminative pathway (Aβ afferents → S1) extracts spatial and temporal properties (texture, shape, compliance). The affective pathway (CT afferents → posterior insula) evaluates whether the contact is within the biologically optimal range for pleasant touch: velocity 1–10 cm/s, surface temperature within ±2°C of skin temperature (~32°C), and moderate surface roughness (Ra 10–100 μm). Materials with low thermal effusivity (e < 800 W·s^½·m⁻²·K⁻¹) maintain skin-temperature contact and activate the CT pathway positively. Materials with high thermal effusivity (e > 3,000) rapidly draw heat from the skin and produce neutral or aversive affective signals.
higher_order_principle: Dual-channel sensory evaluation applied to touch. Just as the visual system has parallel image-forming and non-visual (ipRGC) pathways (L-I panel), the somatosensory system has parallel discriminative and affective pathways. Architecture engages both, but traditional material specification addresses only the discriminative dimension.

causal_links.evidence_base: Physics: contact temperature = f(skin temp, surface temp, relative effusivity). Wood (e~400): contact temp stays near skin temp. Metal (e~12,000): contact temp drops rapidly toward surface temp.
CT afferents fire maximally at skin temperature ±2°C. Contact with low-effusivity materials (wood) maintains this range → high CT firing. (Morrison et al., 2010; Ackerley et al., 2014)
CT optimal velocity: 1–10 cm/s. Moderate roughness (Ra 10–100 μm) at CT-optimal velocity → maximal pleasant signal. (Löken et al., 2009)
CT afferents project via lamina I to posterior insula, bypassing S1. Demonstrated by Olausson et al. (2002).
Posterior insula integrates CT signals with other interoceptive inputs. CT activation contributes positive valence to overall interoceptive assessment.

scope_conditions: Applies only to body-surface contact zones: handrails, seating, flooring, countertops, walls within reach
CT pathway engagement requires direct skin contact — clothing, shoes, and gloves block CT activation
Velocity-dependent: stationary contact engages thermal dimension only; moving contact engages texture-velocity interaction
Modulated by body region: CT afferent density varies (highest in forearm, face; lower in palm, sole)
moderators: Ambient temperature: in cold environments, high-effusivity materials produce larger contact temperature drop
Prior haptic experience: repeated contact habituates discriminative response but CT affective response habituates more slowly
Age: CT afferent density may decline with age
Expectation: visual prediction of material warmth (AX5) modulates surprise but not CT firing rate

interactions.nature: MAT1 provides specific afferent pathway (CT → posterior insula) for one component of interoceptive comfort
Visual appearance generates haptic prediction. MAT1 describes what happens when actual haptic contact occurs.
T8 describes postural affordances; MAT1 adds the affective dimension of the surface that affords contact.
